messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Rajan is a 49-year-old South Asian man who has spent the better part of his adult life as a military medic, a career built on the premise that he could hold others together under the worst imaginable conditions. He is married, though the marriage has grown strained in ways he struggles to articulate, and it was his wife who ultimately persuaded him to seek help after months of watching him disappear into himself. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 56, and what he describes in the first sessions arrives haltingly, in fragments, as though the words themselves are refusing to cooperate.

The abuse was perpetrated by a former partner, a woman he was with for nearly three years before his current marriage. He has never spoken about it in those terms before — *abuse* — and the word sits uncomfortably in his mouth. What he can describe, though not in any linear sequence, is the physical reality of it: being struck, being held down, the particular smell of her sweat during the moments she became violent, the way certain blows landed in his ribs and jaw. He had told himself, and others, that it was complicated. She had faced no consequences. As far as he knows, she has continued her life without interruption, and he had come to understand this not as an injustice but as confirmation of something worse — that perhaps he had not been worth protecting, that something in his constitution had made this possible, had made him deserving of it in some way he could not name but could not stop believing.

The symptoms did not arrive all at once. In the months following the relationship's end, he threw himself back into his work, which in a military medical context meant long shifts, controlled chaos, and the useful numbness of procedure. But over time, certain things began to accumulate. Colleagues who raised their voices during drills. The smell of a fellow medic after a long exercise. These moments would pull him somewhere he did not want to go, and what frightened him most was that when the memory returned it did not feel like remembering — it felt like being back inside it, with the physical sensation of impact returning in his ribs, a tightening in his jaw that had no present-day cause. He cannot find words for what the memory is. When asked to describe the event in session, he goes quiet in a way that is not reluctance but something more like blankness, as though the experience exists in a register that language cannot reach.

He stopped exercising. This was not a conscious decision so much as a discovered boundary — the first time he pushed through a run and felt his own sweat soaking through his shirt, the smell of it triggered something so immediate and physical that he turned back and did not try again. He began avoiding the communal areas of the base, finding reasons to complete paperwork alone, eating at odd hours. He avoided family gatherings, particularly those where certain relatives — people who had known him during that relationship, who might look at him with knowledge or pity — would be present. He rotated through three or four sets of clothes, having quietly retired anything that resembled what he had worn during that period, though he could not have explained the logic to anyone without it sounding strange. These habits formed slowly and then became the architecture of his days.

He sleeps poorly, lying awake with a vigilance he recognises from deployment but that now has no tactical object. Ordinary sounds — a door, a voice in the corridor — bring him upright. He feels safe, genuinely safe, only in his car and in one room of his house, and he is aware that this is not a sustainable perimeter. At work, the presence of senior officers or MPs moving through the ward produces a tension he cannot account for rationally but cannot override.

What finally brought him in was a moment at a family gathering when a relative — someone who had known her — walked through the door, and Rajan found himself unable to stay in the room. He left without explanation. Driving home, he thought: *nothing in my life feels like mine anymore.* He is most afraid, he says, that this is simply who he is now. He is hoping, though he does not quite believe it yet, to be told otherwise.
